To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
There is currently no measure of self-reported medication non-adherence that is suitable for use in primary care to monitor the effectiveness of interventions to improve adherence.
There is a need for an adherence measure which can be completed by or with the help of carers.

there are few self reported adherence measures that are suitable for routine clinical use; the majority of measures are lengthy; there is a lack of validation data for many measures; there is a dearth of data on the time taken to complete measures and on their ability to be completed in conjunction with carer(s); and, while there are a number of measures that can be used to monitor general adherence, there is a paucity of measures that can distinguish between different types and causes of non-adherence
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of such a measure, the Adherence to Drugs in Primary Care (ADIP) questionnaire, and a study to test its reliability and validity.
the development and evaluation of a measure which meets the criteria for use in routine clinical practice.

the development of a self report adherence measure for routine clinical use which is brief, acceptable to the patient, valid, reliable and able to be used in conjunction with carer where necessary, and which has the ability to distinguish different types of non adherence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no measures currently available which meet the criteria for routine use in primary care.
there is no self-reported measure which is suitable for use in routine clinical care and that the most suitable measures are those which are short and easy to complete.
there is no self report measure available which is suitable for this purpose.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a brief, valid, reliable and sensitive measure is required which can be used with or in conjunction with a carer.
the best measure for this purpose is one which can be used with patients or carers, is brief, can distinguish between different types, and has been shown to have acceptable reliability and validity.
there are no measures currently available which meet all our criteria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a self-report measure which meets the criteria for clinical use is yet to be developed.
a measure should be able to distinguish between the two types of non-adherent patients, intentional and unintentional.
the most suitable measures for routine clinical use are likely to be brief, simple to use and able to differentiate between types of non-adherences.
